title: Deep Compositional Phase Diffusion for Long Motion Sequence Generation

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text cites “Johnson et al. [41]” and “recent work in neural phase modeling [42],” including a claimed “up to 70%” artifact reduction. The reference list ends at [40]; entries [41] and [42] do not exist. These claims are therefore untraceable and the citations must be corrected or supplied.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2, “Motion Phase Modeling,” claim attributed to Holden et al. [16]
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper says the fixed-window convolution scheme in PAE “as noted by Holden et al. [16]” introduces instability. Reference [16] is Holden et al., “Phase-Functioned Neural Networks for Character Control” (2017), whereas PAE/DeepPhase is a later 2022 method [15]. Holden et al. could not have identified instability in PAE's fixed-window convolution design. This is a temporal and attribution error.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.1.1, ACT-PAE latent definitions and Eq. (1)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The manuscript states that F, A, B, and S are each in R^4 and are “a scalar value per motion segment,” but then claims Eq. (1) produces Q in R^(N×Q). Scalar phase parameters can only produce a scalar signal per frame, not Q channels. The appendix further says Q=512 is both the latent dimension and the number of periodic signals. To yield an N×512 signal, each of F, A, B, and S must have compatible 512-channel dimensions (or an explicitly specified mapping), which is not what the method states.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.1.1, Eq. (1) and immediately following explanation
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Equation (1) defines Q = A sin(F·T + S) + B, but the prose directly below says the sine function parameterizes “F·(T − S).” These are not equivalent definitions of phase shift: F(T−S)=FT−FS, while the displayed equation is FT+S. The frequency scaling and sign of S differ. One formulation must be corrected.

The main text repeatedly labels SPDM/TPDM outputs as clean latents P^0, e.g. P_pc^0 = F_S(...) and says the modules “estimate” clean phase latents. However, Appendix A.3 explicitly states that both are epsilon-models trained with L1 loss to predict diffusion noise epsilon, and gives losses ||F_S(...)−epsilon||_1 and ||F_T(... )−epsilon||_1. Thus Eq. (2) and Algorithm 1 label and mix epsilon predictions as P^0 clean-latent estimates. A DDIM scheduler can accept epsilon predictions, but then these quantities must be identified as epsilon/model outputs rather than clean latents; the stated mathematical pipeline is internally inconsistent.

The text says “The weighting parameter α controls the balance between transition and semantic information, where α = 0.5 for all segments.” Equation (2) contains no α, only r, and the accompanying algorithm likewise contains no α. The only fixed 0.5-like operation is an unlabelled average of forward and backward transition predictions. Therefore α is undefined and has no specified computational role.

The authors pretrain ACT-PAE on the “full HumanML3D dataset (14,616 sequences)” before BABEL-TEACH fine-tuning, while stating that baseline methods were trained “exclusively on BABEL-TEACH.” This is unequal training data and invalidates the paper's repeated implication of an equal-data/fair comparison. It also directly conflicts with the subsequent statement: “all models being compared are trained on the same dataset and representation.” Evaluation under identical inference conditions does not remedy unequal pretraining data.

The manuscript says BABEL has a maximum length of 250 frames and cites BABEL [4] in support: “datasets like HumanML3D [6] and BABEL [4], with maximum frames of 196 and 250, respectively.” BABEL is an annotation dataset over AMASS motion sequences and is not intrinsically capped at 250 frames; 250 is later stated to be this paper's preprocessing maximum for subsequences. The claim misattributes a local preprocessing restriction to the cited dataset.

The paper says its method “achieves superior performance across all metrics” and “substantially outperform[s] all baseline methods.” Table 2 contradicts this for semantic text alignment: TEACH has Smt. MMD 3.175, lower/better than Ours at 3.642. The table itself marks the authors' value as second best. The conclusion must be qualified rather than claiming superiority on every metric.

The text states that TEACH's “lower Overall FID score indicates a compromise in motion quality.” FID is explicitly marked with ↓ in Table 1, so lower FID indicates better—not worse—motion realism. TEACH's Overall FID of 1.041 is worse than the authors' 0.782, but it is not its lower value that evidences compromised quality. The metric-direction interpretation is backwards.

The abstract claims the framework “completely eliminates” transition issues, produces “flawless transitions in all tested scenarios,” and ensures “perfect boundary alignment.” The reported experiments contain nonzero FID, L2, NPSS, and RMS-Jerk errors, and do not provide a test of exact/perfect boundary equality. These absolute claims are unsupported by the presented evidence and materially overstate the results.
